20008-the-young-duke:
The Young Duke was Disraeli's novel of 1831, a tale of fashionable life. Its hero inherits a dukedom, wealth, and every temptation young. The Countess in these pages had accepted a diamond bracelet the year before. Such gifts map the novel's world of favors and debts. The Lord Viscount St. Maurice stands as future chief of the Fitz-Pompey house. Names themselves arrive dressed for the season. Disraeli wrote society from inside its ballrooms.

Disraeli was twenty-six, dandified, and in debt when he wrote it. The silver-fork novel, fiction of high life, was his first stage. Dukes, races, and romances fill The Young Duke knowingly. Later statesmanship makes the frivolity fascinating. Hints of ambition already glitter under the pleasure. It is a prime minister's juvenilia, shameless and bright.
20809-archie-s-mistake:
Mill hands at Longcross guard their place with pride in Archie's Mistake. New men they dislike get no peace until they quit the Fairfax mills. To belong there counts as a prize the old hands grant with care.

G. A. Henty wrote tales of mill and factory life under the name here tied to Archie. A wrong step by a newcomer sparks the strife of the tale. Work, pride, and fairness clash on the shop floor. The story shows a less known side of its era's fiction, where mills, not battlefields, test a young man's grit and growth.
21487-the-boy-who-sailed-with-blake:
Robert Blake, the great admiral of the Commonwealth, anchors W. H. G. Kingston's The Boy Who Sailed with Blake. Blake lived from 1599 to 1657 and came late to the sea. He defended Bristol, Lyme Regis, and Taunton in the Civil War before taking command afloat.

Kingston frames the history as a page from the fight for civil and religious liberty. A boy's view carries readers through Blake's wars with Prince Rupert and the Dutch. Blake broke Dutch power at Portland and swept the Barbary coast. The tale avoids cheap heroics, aiming instead at sober pride in hard duty.
21703-silver-lake:
Deep in the North American backwoods, hunter Robin Gore builds a new home for his family in this adventure novel by R. M. Ballantyne. Robin grows tired of settlement life as crowds close in around his hamlet. He moves his wife, his son Roy, and his daughter Nelly hundreds of miles into the wild woods, past the last farms.

His nephew Walter and an Irishman named Larry O'Dowd go along to build the new settlement. The family raises three wooden huts and rings them with a stockade for safety. Ballantyne knew the northern woods from his own years in Canada, and the hunting, weather, and daily work here feel close and real.
23256-the-king-of-beaver-and-beaver-ligh:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's The King of Beaver and Beaver Lights comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories. Its subject is James Strang, who styled himself King and Prophet of a peculiar sect on Beaver Island. In the state legislature, Strang had learned how to handle men in the mass.

Nature had also doubly fitted him to entrance women, the tale notes. The spiritual side of Strang appealed most to the one listener best able to appreciate him. Catherwood treats a real island kingdom with a storyteller's eye. Readers get frontier faith, ambition, and charm mixed in one unsettling figure.
262-the-collected-poems-of-rupert-brooke:
Rupert Brooke died in the Aegean in April 1915, aged twenty-seven, and became a symbol of a lost generation. The Collected Poems, in the 1915 edition, gathers his lyrics with an introduction by George Edward Woodberry and a biographical note. Brooke's life runs from Rugby to Cambridge to war.

His poems move from love and youth to the soldier's sonnets that made him famous. An appendix adds poems written about or to Brooke by others. The volume preserves the vivid, charming voice his friends recalled. It remains a poignant record of promise cut short.
574-poems-of-william-blake:
William Blake's Songs of Innocence and of Experience anchor this poetry volume, with The Book of Thel beside them. The Shepherd, The Echoing Green, and the piper's opening song set the innocent world: lambs, children, and green fields under a kind shepherd. Experience answers with darker songs of city, church, and woe.

Blake writes in short, musical lines, pairing innocence and experience as two contrary states of the soul. His plain diction hides deep vision. The book serves as a fine entry to Blake, where a child's song can carry a prophet's charge.
868-the-philosopher-s-joke:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this short tale that opens with the narrator's frank doubt: he does not believe the story himself. Six persons, he says, are persuaded of its truth, and their hope is to convince themselves and others that a philosopher's joke can carry real weight. The joke itself turns on a trick of thought.

Jerome lets the tale hover between jest and earnest, with his usual light touch. The fun lies in watching sober folk defend an absurdity, and in the narrator's refusal to join them. The piece is brief and witty, a small example of Jerome's gift for turning a parlour paradox into a story.
by-pike-and-dyke: By Pike and Dyke, G. A. Henty's Dutch revolt tale. The pikemen. This book preserves that historical novel. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnes-mary-cl:
Agnes Mary Clerke was an astronomer born at Skibbereen, County Cork, on 10 February 1842. She died in London on 20 January 1907. She showed marked interest in astronomy from the start of her study. Before fifteen she had begun writing that science's history. Dublin took the family in 1861, Queenstown in 1863. Later she went to Italy, staying chiefly at Florence until 1877, studying at the public library.

London became her home in 1877. Her first important article, Copernicus in Italy, appeared in the Edinburgh Review that October. She won world-wide reputation in 1885 with A Popular History of Astronomy in the Nineteenth Century, at once recognized as authoritative. Though not a practical astronomer, she passed three months at the Cape Observatory in 1888 as Sir David Gill's guest, gaining familiarity with spectroscopic work. In 1892 the Royal Institution awarded her its Actonian Prize of one hundred guineas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-larke:
Blessed John Larke, an English martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. He died at Tyburn on 7 March 1544 after a long parish career: rector of St. Ethelburga's, Bishopsgate, from 1505, of Woodford from 1527, and of Chelsea from 1530, on Thomas More's presentation. More's parish priest and personal friend, he is styled doctor, though his faculty is unknown.

Indicted in February 1544 with German Gardiner, John Ireland, and John Heywood, he was condemned for denying the royal supremacy. Heywood recanted on the hurdle and lived, while Larke, Gardiner, and Ireland suffered together at Tyburn, their heads and quarters buried under the gallows. The entry presents a parish priest caught in Henry's last terror.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-burke:
Edmund Burke was the first Vicar Apostolic of Nova Scotia, born in County Kildare in 1753 and dead at Halifax in 1820. Barred from study at home by the penal laws, he trained in Paris, then sailed to Canada in 1786 and taught philosophy and mathematics at the Quebec seminary. He longed for mission work, and in 1794 he was sent to Upper Canada.

For seven years he rode a hard pioneer circuit among scattered Catholics, and he spoke plainly about race prejudice hurting the faith. Sent to Halifax in 1801, he became Vicar-General of Nova Scotia in 1815 and Bishop of Zion in 1818. The entry credits him with steady work for faith, schooling, and civic life in the early years of the province.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ellen-mary-cl:
Ellen Mary Clerke was an Irish journalist and novelist, sister of Agnes Mary Clerke, born at Skibbereen in 1840 and dead in London in 1906. A gifted writer, she served for many years as an editorial writer for the London Tablet. She had a striking grasp of the religious and political tangles of continental Europe. Seven years in Italy made her at home in its language, literature, and public life.

She sent Florence periodicals a series of stories perfect in Italian phrase, idiom, and local colour. Her pamphlets Jupiter and His System and The Planet Venus added to popular astronomy. In 1899 she published Fable and Song in Italy. It holds essays and studies with Italian poems turned into English in their original metres. Her last work was the novel Flowers of Fire, issued in 1902.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-of-sai:
The Gospel of Saint Luke opens with a biography of Saint Luke, probably an abbreviation of Lucanus, generally held a native of Antioch. Eusebius calls him a physician who lived long and closely with Paul and knew the other apostles well. A Catholic Encyclopedia article treats the Gospel's authenticity, integrity, purpose, contents, sources, and accuracy.

The article also takes up disputed points: Lysanias, Tetrarch of Abilene, who spoke the Magnificat, the census of Quirinius, and Luke's relation to Josephus. The writer's special interest in Antioch and acquaintance with it appear in Acts, where the city recurs again and again. Luke's name itself seems unknown before the Christian Era, though Lucanus is common in inscriptions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-von-:
Medieval poet Heinrich von Veldeke, a knight born near Maastricht about the middle of the twelfth century, pioneered courtly romance in Germany. Learned in Latin and French and familiar with Virgil and Ovid, he first wrote a legend of St. Servatius for a Countess of Looz, then turned to his great Eneide on Aeneas and Dido.

Most of the Eneide was done by 1175 at Cleves when its manuscript, lent to a countess, was carried to Thuringia. After nine years he recovered and finished it under Hermann of Saxony before 1190. Based on an old French romance and thoroughly medievalized around love, it fixed the short rhyming couplet, strict metre, pure rhyme, and courtly style that later epic writers followed. His lyrics brought French forms into Minnesong.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-lemcke:
Henry Lemcke, a missionary in the United States, was born at Rhena in Mecklenburg in 1796, converted from Protestant preaching to Catholicism in 1824, and was ordained at Ratisbon in 1826. Coming to America in 1834, he served briefly at Holy Trinity in Philadelphia, then assisted the aged Prince Gallitzin at Loretto, Pennsylvania, from Ebensburg, covering some fifty miles. In 1838 he laid out Carrolltown, named for John Carroll, the United States' first Catholic bishop, succeeding Gallitzin at Loretto in 1840.

Lemcke brought the first Benedictines to America under Boniface Wimmer, future archabbot of St. Vincent's, and joined the new community himself in 1852. In 1855 he travelled as missionary to Kansas, opening the way for St. Benedict's Abbey at Atchison, then served at Elizabeth, New Jersey, from 1861 to 1877, spending his remaining years at Carrolltown, where he died in 1882. He also wrote a life of Prince Gallitzin, published at Münster in 1861.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-ernst-ja:
Karl Ernst Jarcke was born at Danzig in 1801, of a Protestant merchant family, and died at Vienna in 1852. He studied jurisprudence and taught criminal law at Bonn and later at Berlin. His Handbuch des gemeinen deutschen Strafrechts appeared in three volumes from 1827 to 1830. Longing for faith, he became a Catholic at Cologne in 1824.

His anonymous brochure on the French Revolution of 1830 won the approval of the crown prince's anti-revolutionary circle. He edited their Politische Wochenblatt from 1831, and Metternich called him to Vienna's State Chancery in 1832. In 1837 he parted from his Berlin friends over the Cologne Occurrence, the archbishop's imprisonment, which they approved and he condemned. His ideal was the medieval Germanic state, with a hereditary monarch and a state confined to war and justice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-proske:
Karl Proske was born at Grobing in Upper Silesia in 1794 and died in 1861. After a Halle medical doctorate he became court physician at Oppeln and served as an army surgeon in 1813 to 1815. He also loved ecclesiastical chant with enthusiasm. In 1821 he resolved on the priesthood, and Ratisbon ordained him in April 1826.

From then on he gave himself to ancient church music, spending his income and preferments on searching Italian and other archives. In 1830 he became canon and Kapellmeister of Ratisbon cathedral, where he had sung as vicar choral since 1827. Patiently he gathered and copied hundreds of musical scores. In 1853 he began his Musica Divina, whose fourth volume appeared in 1862, followed by his two-volume Selectus Novus Missarum of 1857 to 1861.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luke-joseph-h: This 1913 reference piece on Hooke — the Sorbonne theologian. Andrew MacErlean honors his famous works. His pen taught the Paris schools. The university prized its learned son. The eighteenth century knew his name. His 1796 death is famed. His 1796 works are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-locke: A 1913 entry on Locke — the English composer. William Grattan-Flood honors his famous music. His choir crowned the Restoration court. The age prized the gifted hand. The churches keep his name. His 1677 death is famed. His 1677 music is famed. His 1677 court anthems are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-henry: Patrick Henry O'Rorke was the Irish-American colonel who died leading his men at Gettysburg. This entry traces his career, his courage, and his death. The hero of Little Round Top: his gallant charge saved the Union's exposed left flank that day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-majunke: This biographical entry profiles Paul Majunke, a German priest and journalist of the 1800s, tracing his career, his press work, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's German gallery, preserved among its early modern churchmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pembroke: Pembroke, the Welsh town of the great castle, has its own Catholic history of missions and parishes. This entry covers its churches and institutions as of 1913. The faith in the land of the castles: its quiet parishes serve Pembrokeshire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-aske: Robert Aske was the leader of the Pilgrimage of Grace. This entry traces his rising, his pardon, and his execution. The captain of the northern host: his white banner bore the Wounds of Christ in 1536's autumn of revolt and hope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-bicker: Robert Bickerdike was the Yorkshire martyr of Elizabeth's reign. This entry notes his constancy, his trial, and his death. The layman of the scaffold: his staunch faith defied the judge at York in 1586's spring of persecution and fear and hate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-dymoke: Robert Dymoke was the Lincolnshire martyr of Elizabeth's reign. This entry notes his constancy, his trial, and his death. The gentleman of the scaffold: his staunch faith defied Elizabeth's laws in 1580's September at Lincoln's assizes of the north in autumn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salt-lake: Salt Lake became the diocese of Utah's capital. This entry covers its bishops, its parishes, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the Mormon city: its stone cathedral crowns the town in Utah's valley in the west of the state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sampson-erdes: Sampson Erdeswicke was the antiquary of Staffordshire. This entry notes his survey, his manuscripts, and his fame. The historian of the English shires: his learned survey mapped Staffordshire in the 1590s' England in the shires of the Midlands' heart in the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sherbrooke: Sherbrooke became the diocese of Quebec's Eastern Townships. This entry covers its bishops, its churches, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the St. Francis river: its stone churches serve the townships in Quebec's Eastern Townships in the province.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-burke: Burke was the Dominican of the pulpit. This long entry examines his 1800s, his America, and his sermons. The preacher of the Irish people: his fiery sermons crowned America in the 1870s of the missions in the very old cities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-nichol: Burke was the Dominican of the pulpit. This long entry examines his 1800s, his America, and his sermons. The preacher of the Irish people: his fiery sermons crowned America in the 1870s of the missions in the very old cities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-willia: Croke was the archbishop of Cashel. This long entry examines his 1800s, his Thurles, and his see. The primate of the Munster church: his proud Thurles crowned Tipperary in the 1870s of the Land League in the very old fields.
doe-osti-17026347-wdh-dataset-ai-readine: Making datasets AI-ready got its intake form, and this WDH document standardizes machine-actionability documentation. The pages set the curator's checklist. The data stewards get their form. Version one was released. The checklist was version one. The stewards got forms.
doe-osti-3020472-close-out-project-descr: Koepke's grant got close-out-described, and this DOE DE-SC0021405 text wraps the project. The pages detail the findings. The researchers get their data. The grant was Koepke's. The data were researcher. The DE-SC0021405 was grant. The close-out was project.
doe-osti-3376722-seismic-velocity-modeli: NNSS got seismic-relocated, and this DOE text models southern Nevada. The pages detail the velocity findings. The geologists get their data. The site was national security. The data were geologist. The NNSS were relocations. The southern were Nevada. The modeling were velocity.
doe-osti-3377646-marine-fuel-innovation-: Great Lakes got fuel-innovated, and this DOE slides cover marine fuels. The pages detail the innovation findings. The transport folks get their deck. The seaway was St Lawrence. The deck was transport. The lakes were great. The St were Lawrence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NewmanSamMike_N:
An FBI memorandum dated November 25, 1963 concerns Sam Mike Newman of New Orleans. Newman owned the property at 544 Camp Street. Agents reported on Cubans seen there, in company with associates of Guy Banister. Banister, a former FBI man turned private investigator, ran his office at that address.

544 Camp Street became one of the most examined addresses in the case. Oswald had stamped it on leaflets he handed out for a pro-Castro group. A memo written three days after the assassination shows agents already working the building's tenants and visitors. Newman's name enters the record as landlord, a small part in a building that would not leave the story.
govdocs-archive_org-politica-aeterna-ale: Aleksandr Dugin's Politica Aeterna treats politics as metaphysics. Its subtitle names the two poles of the book: political Platonism and what Dugin calls the Black Enlightenment. The work belongs to his Noomachia: Wars of the Mind series. Dugin, a Russian philosopher, builds a system in which ideas and myths fight for the future. The volume presents that system at length for readers of his political philosophy.
govdocs-archive_org-the-history-of-etrur: The History of Etruria, Volume 1: the volume - the declassified government document, subject: government records, a single volume, dated material, filed. An obscure item, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the literature and readers.
hassan-the-story-of-hassan-of-bagdad-and:
James Elroy Flecker, an English poet and diplomat, set his play Hassan in Baghdad of the Arabian Nights. Hassan, a confectioner of forty-five, boils sugar in his sweetshop and dreams of elsewhere. His friend Selim teases the longings out of him in the scene. Flecker builds the play in five acts of song-filled verse.

The Caliph Haroun ar Raschid walks the city with his minstrel Ishak, vizier Jafar, and executioner Masrur. Rafi, King of the Beggars, and the girl Yasmin cross Hassan's path as court and street collide. Pervaneh, Hassan's love, grounds his dreaming in shop and home. Gifts from the Caliph turn to terror as Hassan sees how power amuses itself with pain. At last he quits Baghdad on the golden journey to Samarkand. Flecker's play, staged after his death, became known for its caravan finale and its warning that beauty and cruelty share one throne.
joe-s-luck-or-always-wide-awake:
Joe's Luck, or Always Wide Awake, is a boys' novel by Horatio Alger Jr., printed in a 1913 New York edition. Alger wrote many such tales, including Tony the Tramp, The Cash Boy, and Do and Dare. Chapter one introduces Joe, a stout boy of fifteen with an honest, sun-browned face. He works as a servant in the Norton household.

The book opens with a small act of defiance. Oscar Norton orders Joe to brush him off, and Joe flatly refuses. He says he will not be ordered round, though Oscar calls it impudence and asks if he has turned lazy. Joe's firm stand sets the pattern for Alger's hero: poor, proud, and awake to every chance.
kindness-to-animals-or-the-sin-of-cruelt:
Kindness to Animals is Charlotte Elizabeth's book for children, issued by the American Sunday-School Union at Philadelphia. It was entered according to Congress's act in 1845. The first chapter explains the plan: this is not natural history. Elizabeth tells only of animals she has known and watched herself since childhood.

Nothing appears in the book, she promises, that is not exactly true so far as she knows. Watching animals kept her mind busy in early life, and she commends the habit to children. Incidents from her own animals carry the lessons in kindness. Elizabeth, a popular religious writer, taught mercy to dumb creatures as a Christian duty. Her little book belongs to the Sunday-school shelf of improving tales for the young.
krindlesyke:
Wilfrid Wilson Gibson published Krindlesyke with Macmillan in London in 1922. It is a long dramatic poem in two books. Gibson notes that an early draft of Book One appeared in 1910.

He rewrote that first book completely for this edition. Book Two, written from 1919 to 1922, had not been printed before. Gibson says the work was not planned for the stage. He flavors the speech with local northern words, mostly words of feeling that readers can grasp from context. North country speech and farm life ground the poem's drama. Gibson lets plain voices carry grief, love, and stubborn pride.
may-brooke:
Anna Hanson Dorsey wrote May Brooke, held in rights by P. J. Kenedy in 1888. The book also bears the name Conscience, or, The Trials of May Brooke. Uncle Stillinghast and May herself lead the first two chapters.

A morning errand, Aunt Mabel, and tales of past and present follow. Troubled waters, trials, and a warning test the young heroine. A midnight messenger, a new will, and a secret sin deepen the plot. Repentance appears twice in the heads, and remorse stands near the end. Helen gets a chapter of her own amid the trials. Faith and conscience steer the plot more than wealth or rank.
mike:
P. G. Wodehouse published Mike, a public school story, in London in 1909. Its hero, Mike Jackson, arrives at school already famous for cricket. The frontispiece quotes a fan asking about his batting average of fifty-one. Twelve full-page illustrations by T. M. R. Whitwell accompany the text.

Early chapters cover the journey down, the nets, and a row with the town. Mike finds friends, scrapes, and a great picnic in his first terms. Wodehouse writes about Wrykyn school life with affection and comic timing. The novel began his long series of school and cricket stories, and introduced readers to his lightest manner.
miss-merivale-s-mistake:
Mrs. Henry Clarke opens this novel with a startling discovery. Miss Merivale, tired from the long drive from Woodcote, half-dozes while two girls talk at the window. A name, Rhoda Sampson, makes her sit bolt upright with anxious curiosity. The frontispiece shows Pauline Smythe studying a photograph frame.

Pauline's diplomacy and suspicions drive much of the plot. Tom and Rhoda meet, invitations are issued, and a confession follows. A visit to Kentish Town and the figure of Polly Smith deepen the mystery of identities. Clarke writes a Victorian tale of mistaken names, family secrets, and an older woman's error.
my-lady-nicotine-a-study-in-smoke:
J. M. Barrie wrote these light essays on smoking, his lady Nicotine. M. B. Prendergast drew the pictures for the Boston edition. Chapter one compares matrimony and smoking, to comic effect. My first cigar and the Arcadia mixture follow.

Barrie writes of his pipes, pouch, and smoking table with mock care. Friends like Gilray, Marriot, and Jimmy fill the middle chapters. A houseboat named Arcadia hosts more smoke and talk. The romance of a pipe cleaner gets its own tale. Barrie turns a small habit into bright, whimsical prose, years before Peter Pan made him most famous.
never-fail-blake:
Arthur Stringer wrote Never-Fail Blake, a mystery issued in New York with a 1913 copyright by the Bobbs-Merrill Company. The book was sold under the banner Supertales of Modern Mystery. Its frontispiece shows a suitor asking, then why can't you marry me?

Blake serves as a second deputy, and the tale opens in his office. A woman named Elsie walks in, silk rustling, and sits at the end of his desk. Blake greets her without looking up, in a gloomy, hound eyed mood. Old ties between the two hang over the talk. Crime, office work, and a past romance drive Stringer's story from there.
on-a-torn-away-world-or-the-captives-of-:
Roy Rockwood wrote this boys' adventure in the Great Marvel series. Other series titles promise trips to both poles and Mars. The contents open with a chapter called Shot Into the Air. Mark hangs on in the second chapter's title. A great earthquake tears the heroes' world apart.

Courage and quick thinking help the young heroes survive. Rockwood wrote fast, fantastic tales for young readers. The book belongs with early science adventure for boys. Peril follows peril in a strange, broken landscape. It is pure thrill fiction of its period.
podcast-dannyjones-bq3Y0qE7AKE:
Brigham Buhler joins Danny Jones to argue that doctors are barred by law from telling patients the full truth. The episode title calls him a pharma whistleblower. Buhler speaks from his work in health care and his break with the drug trade.

Buhler claims drug firms hide cures and punish doctors who step out of line. He names the rules and fears that keep doctors quiet, as he sees them. Jones asks which claims rest on paper he can show. Listeners get a sharp charge against the drug trade from a man who worked in it. The library files the talk as an archive record.
podcast-dannyjones-vD0y4xUxnKE:
Diane Hennacy joins Danny Jones to tell how she saw a test that should not be possible. The episode title bills her as a Harvard doctor. Her tale centers on a mind test with results that broke the rules she knew.

Hennacy tells the tale in full, from the setup of the test to the score that stunned the room. She talks about what the result did to her view of the mind. Jones asks what checks were run to rule out tricks. Listeners get a quiet, strange story told by a trained mind. The library holds the talk as an archive record of her account.
podcast-joerogan-2DGXoLiwLkE:
Dr. Shanna Swan joins Joe Rogan for episode 1638 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Swan is an epidemiologist who studies how chemicals in daily goods harm fertility. Her book warned of a steep fall in sperm counts in the West.

Swan lays out her finds on plastics, sprays, and the parts of the body they bend. She argues the harm starts in the womb and builds for life. Rogan asks what a man can cut from his home now. Listeners get a grave health talk with steps they can take. The library keeps the episode as a record of her stated work.
podcast-joerogan-KoM8f5Gp3kE:
Psychedelic research pioneer Amanda Feilding joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2002. Feilding founded the Beckley Foundation and spent decades funding studies the mainstream would not touch, from LSD brain scans to cannabis policy. Few people have done more to restart the field.

She tells Rogan how she began, what the early scans showed, and where she wants the research to go next. Rogan asks about her famous self-experiments and the cost of working outside the academy. The episode is a rare long hearing with the woman many scientists credit for psychedelic science's return.
podcast-tuckercarlson-_QV7WpLaHkE:
Veteran Braxton McCoy joins Tucker Carlson to talk Iraq, opioids, and defending American land. McCoy was wounded in Iraq, then fought opioid addiction after coming home. He later became a voice for keeping US land out of foreign and corporate hands.

McCoy tells his war story and the harder battle with pain pills that followed. He explains how foreign governments and giant firms are buying farmland and why he resists it. Carlson connects the fights into one veteran's triple battle, abroad and at home. Patriots and the concerned get a plain, hard-earned perspective.
poems-of-william-blake:
William Blake's poems appear here in his two great song cycles, the Songs of Innocence and of Experience, together with the Book of Thel. Blake etched and printed these books himself in the late eighteenth century, selling a handful of copies while London ignored him. The Innocence songs open with a piper commanded by a laughing child on a cloud to pipe a song about a lamb. Then to write his happy songs in a book every child may read.

The Shepherd follows, praising the sweet lot of a life spent praising among the sheep. Experience answers Innocence poem by poem, with the same world seen through loss, anger, and knowledge. Thel, a young spirit hesitating before birth and experience, closes the volume in dialogue with the small creatures of her vale. No short book in English holds more per page.
selections-from-the-speeches-and-writing:
Edmund Burke's speeches and writings fill this chosen volume, fronted by a long opening essay on his life and rank. The essay places Burke high in what it calls the aristocracy of mind. It records his birth at Dublin in 1730, his attorney father, and his boyhood schooling in the country.

Burke entered Trinity College and rose to fame as a speaker of rare force and moral weight. The essay quotes Quintilian on the orator as a good man, whose words carry a judge's trust. Readers get both Burke's own pages and a portrait of the statesman whom later ages kept honoring.
seneca-naturales-quaestiones-clarke:
John Clarke translated Seneca's Naturales Quaestiones in 1910 as Physical Science in the Time of Nero. Seneca, the Stoic philosopher and Nero's adviser, wrote the work around 62 CE. It is the Roman encyclopedia of natural phenomena.

Lightning, earthquakes, comets, rainbows, and the Nile's floods all receive books. Seneca asks how nature works and how a wise person should meet it. He gathers Greek science into Latin with moral reflections attached. Comets, then feared as omens, get a calm and rational treatment. Clarke's translation keeps the Stoic's curiosity bright for English readers. The work shows Roman science at its most inquiring before Seneca's forced death.
sonnets-and-sonnets-on-english-dramatic-: Algernon Charles Swinburne's Sonnets and his Sonnets on English Dramatic Poets (1590-1650) are taken from Volume V of his Collected Poetical Works. The 1917 Heinemann issue at London notes a first printing by Chatto in 1904, with reprints through 1912. The opening list of sonnets names Hope and Fear, After Sunset, and A Study from Memory, then sonnets to Dr. John Brown and to William Bell Scott, and A Death on Easter Day.
tales-of-the-chesapeake:
Geo. Alfred Townsend, who signed his work Gath, published Tales of the Chesapeake in New York in 1880. Townsend gave the book to his father and noted that his kin had first come to Chesapeake Bay in 1623 and settled on the Pocomoke River.

Townsend says two pieces, Kidnapped and Dominion over the Fish, had run in Chambers's Journal in London. A poem, Herman of Bohemia Manor, is new, and all the pieces share one bay region. Readers get verse and prose steeped in oyster fleets, old houses, and local lore, from a writer who knew the shore as home ground.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-42-luk:
Luke , read in the King James Version, begins with a writer's preface. Many, he says, have taken in hand to set out in order a declaration of things most surely believed among them.

Those accounts were delivered by eyewitnesses and ministers of the word from the beginning. It seemed good to Luke also, with perfect understanding from the first, to write in order to Theophilus. His aim is certainty about what Theophilus was taught. The narrative then turns to Herod's days and a priest named Zacharias, whose wife Elisabeth was of the daughters of Aaron.
the-collected-poems-of-rupert-brooke:
Rupert Brooke's collected poems appear here in a 1915 edition, with an introduction by George Edward Woodberry and a biographical note by Margaret Lavington. A short life record heads the book. Brooke was born at Rugby on August 3, 1887, and became a Fellow of King's College, Cambridge, in 1913.

He took a commission as a sub-lieutenant in the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve in September 1914 and joined the Antwerp expedition that October. He sailed with the British Mediterranean Expeditionary Force on February 28, 1915, and died in the Aegean on April 23, 1915. Woodberry's introduction dwells on his vivid life. Brooke was fair to see and winning in his ways, Woodberry writes, and above all there was life in him. His senses met the world with surprise and delight, tasting each thing as if it were a fresh discovery. Lavington's note and poems about Brooke close the volume.
the-god-of-his-fathers-tales-of-the-klon:
The God of His Fathers: Tales of the Klondyke gathers short tales. They first ran in magazines such as McClure's, Ainslee's, and Outing. This edition is from Sir Isaac Pitman and Sons, dated 1906. The contents list eleven tales. They run from the title story through Siwash and The Man with the Gash. They name Grit of Women and A Daughter of the Aurora.

The title tale opens on the primeval forest. The old struggle for life still rages there. Briton and Russian overlap in the Land of the Rainbow's End. Yankee gold has not yet bought the land. Wolf packs pull down caribou. Native peoples live under chiefs and medicine men. They drive out bad spirits and fight their neighbors. Into that harsh world the tale brings white men and their faiths.
the-high-school-boys-training-hike:
H. Irving Hancock wrote The High School Boys' Training Hike, subtitled Making Themselves Hard as Nails. Chapter titles include The Deed of a Hero, The Peddler and the Lawyer's Half, The No-Breakfast Plan, Making the Tramps Squirm, and Dick Prescott, Knight Errant. Chapter one opens with Dick Prescott trying to hire a wagon from Mr. Newbegin Titmouse.

Dick offers ten dollars, and Titmouse asks if that means per week. Dick answers no: ten dollars for the whole month of August. Titmouse cries that the sum is absurd for the use of a fine wagon. The haggling sets a comic tone for a hike built around rough travel, peddlers, tramps, and hard training.
the-lady-of-the-lake:
Sir Walter Scott's poem appears here in a Boston school edition of 1883. William J. Rolfe edited it with notes. He had been head master of the High School in Cambridge, Massachusetts. His preface explains his work. He borrowed cuts from an illustrated edition. A cheaper annotated one was his aim. Then he found the text itself troublesome. No two editions agreed exactly. Even Black's Author's Edition was full of misprints.

He compared the first edition of 1810 line by line. A London bookseller supplied it. The Edinburgh edition of 1821 and a dozen others joined the check. He restored first-edition readings where later changes were not Scott's. His examples are precise. Clift had corrupted to cliff, heat to heart. Boune became bound, barded became barbed. The volume serves students reading Scott's Highland romance. Ellen Douglas and the disguised king fill it.
the-lake:
George Moore's novel appears here in a 1921 William Heinemann edition. Its opening pages carry his dedicatory letter in French. Édouard Dujardin is its addressee. The date is August 17, 1905. Moore confesses a theft in it. Busy correcting proofs in Paris, he stole a title. Dujardin's work in progress, La Source du Fleuve Chrétien, supplied it. A character in Moore's novel bears the stolen name. Ralph Elles never appears but is much talked of. The dedication compensates the larceny.

The letter drifts into memory. Decades of talk about literature and music lie behind them. His Confessions of a Young Englishman appeared in Dujardin's Revue Indépendante. Hours at Fontainebleau and Valvins return to him. No orchestra is needed to explain his poor country's sadness, Moore writes. A single flute on an island in a lake suffices. The epistle sets the key for an Irish priest's story.
the-philosopher-s-joke:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote The Philosopher's Joke, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company. The narrator opens by saying he does not believe the story himself. Six persons are persuaded of its truth, and their hope is to convince themselves it was an hallucination. Their trouble is that there are six of them, close friends who cannot get away from one another.

The man who told it, called Armitage, though that is not his real name, confessed it one night in a club smoking room. He hoped the narrator's flippant scepticism would show him the absurd side. Jerome frames a strange tale as a secret its witnesses long to disbelieve, and the narrator promptly, discreetly, tells Mrs. Armitage, who bursts into tears.
the-poems-of-henry-van-dyke: The Poems of Henry Van Dyke is shown here in a new and revised edition with many hitherto uncollected pieces. Arthur F. Bird published it at London in 1925. Here only the title page and a list of the author's books appear, so the poems themselves are absent. That list names prose volumes Little Rivers and Out-of-Doors in the Holy Land. It names story collections The Blue Flower and The Unknown Quantity. Poem volumes such as The White Bees appear too, along with the play The House of Rimmon.
the-songs-of-a-sentimental-bloke:
C. J. Dennis wrote these Australian verse tales of the Sentimental Bloke, a working-class larrikin in love, and a foreword by a fellow writer introduces them warmly. The foreword recalls how the poems, running in the Bulletin, brightened dark days, and calls the Bloke more perfect than any earlier larrikin character, the writer's own beloved Benno included.

Readers meet a man longing to be something better, and Doreen, the girl he courts, whom the foreword praises as standing for all good women. Dennis's slang-filled humour, the foreword warns, can hide the tenderness underneath, so the introduction asks readers to notice both the jokes and the feeling.
the-tempting-of-tavernake:
E. Phillips Oppenheim begins The Tempting of Tavernake on the roof of a grim London boarding-house near Russell Square. A young American girl leans against the railing, staring over the housetops with a gloomy, rebellious expression. Tavernake, uncompromisingly English, has followed her up through the trap-door and stands watching her in silence. They are almost strangers, bound only by boarding-house etiquette and a few greetings.

Below them the painted city stretches to a blood-red horizon as the sun sinks into vaporous cloud. He wonders who she is and why she came friendless to London. Oppenheim builds the opening from watching and guessing: shabby, well-made clothes, tired eyes, and a smouldering fire that marks her as a rebel he means to understand.
the-world-english-bible-web-luke:
Luke's Gospel, book forty-two in the World English Bible, starts with a careful preface. Many had already written narratives of Jesus, Luke notes. Eyewitnesses and servants of the word handed the accounts down. Luke says he traced everything accurately from the first. He writes in order for Theophilus. Certainty about his instruction is the goal.

The story then turns to a priest named Zacharias. His wife Elizabeth descends from Aaron's line. Both live righteously and blamelessly, Luke says. Yet they have no child, and both are old. An angel's visit will interrupt their quiet faithfulness. Readers get the most orderly and literary of the Gospels.
the-young-priest-s-keepsake:
Michael J. Phelan, a Jesuit priest, wrote The Young Priest's Keepsake for a limited clerical audience. His note to the enlarged second edition, printed in Dublin in 1909, marvels at its success. The first edition sold out in little over two months. Its price, he admits, could not be called cheap. Reviewers welcomed the book without a single jarring note, he reports.

Phelan thanks the author of My New Curate for a thoughtful critique. Ecclesiastical colleges forgave his blunt candour in some chapters. They gave the book a more than cordial reception, he says. The keepsake offers frank guidance to newly ordained priests. Its quick sale suggests young clergy wanted practical, honest counsel.
things-to-make: A transcriber's note opens this record by warning that the text alone is of limited use because so many figures matter. Some projects use strong chemicals, sparks, or steam boilers, and lead solder should never touch cooking utensils. A glossary then defines terms such as batten, bevel, bradawl, chamfer, boss, broach, carbide, and creosote. The note addresses a young boy's world of carpentry, machinery, and kites. No author or title page is present here, and no project instructions appear, so only the note and terms are shown.
tom-slade-at-black-lake:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh answered readers in his preface who asked when Tom Slade would grow up and stop being a Scout. Tom is already grown, Fitzhugh says, and will never cease. Once a Scout, always a Scout is the book's motto, published with Boy Scouts of America approval in 1920.

Scouting, he argues, is not measles or a tin steam-engine to discard. It sticks out all over a man, who returns as assistant or scoutmaster. A frontispiece shows Tom hauling logs by block and fall at Black Lake. Readers get a Scout novel whose preface defends lifelong scouting.
vegetius-de-re-militari-clarke:
Vegetius composed De Re Militari, the Military Institutions of the Romans, around 390 CE. John Clarke's English translation appeared in 1767. Vegetius boiled centuries of Roman practice into a handbook for emperors.

Recruiting, training, marching, and siegecraft receive orderly, practical treatment. He laments that the army of his day had let old discipline slip. His famous line says that wanting peace means preparing for war. Medieval generals prized the book above all other military writing. Kings and commanders consulted it for a thousand years after Rome fell. Clarke's version keeps the old reformer's bluntness in plain English.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
Luke's Gospel is book 42 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. Luke tells Theophilus that many have tried to write the story before him. He has traced the facts with care from the start. His goal is an orderly account that the reader can trust.

The story opens in the days of King Herod with a priest named Zechariah. His wife Elizabeth, old and childless, is of Aaron's line. While Zechariah burns incense in the temple, an angel appears at the altar. Fear grips him at the sight. Weymouth's neat prose fits Luke's careful, linked style of telling.
